title: Words Ending in Alif and Hamza
intro: Ibn Durayd makes the ear do the work of a grammar book. A maqsur noun ends in a long a, while a mamdud noun adds a hamza, the catch heard at the end of the rhyme. One pair turns earth into wealth, another gives two names for the same thing. Al-Saeed questions the attribution of three supplementary verses and closes with an extra pair about dreams and outward appearance.

translation: Do not put your trust in desire.
Beware the day you leave the open air.
1.sharh: Desire is something one carries inside, air the space one lives in. The final catch of the voice moves the listener from the first to the second, and from living to burial.

translation: One day you will pass into damp earth,
and someone else will come into the wealth.
2.sharh: The estate has two destinations. Its owner goes underground, while someone who outlives him enjoys what he amassed. The near-identical nouns are assigned to different people.

translation: How many a hollow by the rim
of a well holds someone whose hope ran out.
3.sharh: The Arabic “edge of” reaches across the break for its well. The hollow beside that physical limit becomes a resting place for someone who has reached the limit of expectation.

translation: Over him the flat stones were laid
by people who loved him with undivided hearts.
4.sharh: The people laying down the slabs are identified only in the second half. The burial is the last service his dearest friends can perform for him.

translation: The young man has gone from his family.
What has become of the lad and his youthful prime?
5.sharh: The household has lost an individual. The question that follows separates him from the quality he exemplified, the vigour of being young.

translation: The light has gone out of his eyes.
He has lost the distinction of high rank.
6.sharh: One brightness was his to see by. The other was the distinction by which others recognised him. Repeating “has gone” sets both losses at the same moment.

translation: He kept searching for fresh grass
until he was quite alone in the waste.
7.sharh: The word for green herbage gives him a reason to keep going. Its longer partner takes away everything a traveller might have hoped to find at the end.

translation: Time severed the sinew in his thigh
and granted him no reprieve.
8.sharh: Time strikes at the great nerve or sinew down the thigh. The near echo means postponement, the one benefit Time refuses its victim.

translation: I find that poor sight in the dark most often
comes of the evening meal.
9.sharh: The commentary glosses the second word as supper. The suggestion that supper causes poor night vision belongs to the old mnemonic. Its purpose is to fix two pronunciations in the memory.

translation: I find hunger sharpens the minds
of those who reflect in an empty place.
10.sharh: An empty stomach and an empty dwelling make two different kinds of room for thought. Both nouns come to sound like conditions of the same act of reflection.

translation: Many a man guards the ground around his home,
yet he will be cast into the open.
11.sharh: The protected space is the ground adjoining a house or camp. Control over who may enter it gives no power over where its owner will finally be laid.

translation: Whoever fears the ache of sore feet
should avoid walking barefoot.
12.sharh: One noun names what happens to the feet, the other the condition of walking unshod. The final hamza distinguishes the cause from the pain it can produce.

translation: How many have disappeared beneath a dune
after a life of cleanliness and purity.
13.sharh: Sand hides a body that its owner once took pains to keep clean. The extra word for cleanliness helps the listener hear the abstract sense of the second rhyme.

translation: A man is kin to the wild ass’s foal
if he is forever bent on doing you harm.
14.sharh: “Brother of the foal” is a comparison for the obstinate companion. The second noun means being hooked on something, here doing harm. The commentary also records a wild cow’s calf for the first word.

translation: Life goes hand in hand with rain,
and grace with a sense of shame.
15.sharh: Rain visibly revives the earth. The matching construction asks the listener to recognise a less visible source of human beauty, the ability to feel shame.

translation: The wisdom of an elder among men
shows in the good deeds of his grandchildren.
16.sharh: An elder’s judgement can outlive him in the conduct of his grandchildren. The rhyme ordinarily points behind someone. Here it names the generation that comes after him.

translation: If the sheep knew what flaying meant for her,
she would make haste to escape.
17.sharh: The sheep is imagined foreseeing what will be stripped from her own body. Foresight supplies the motive for flight that the similar-sounding nouns place side by side.

translation: To me, sickness is an illness that lingers.
Do not neglect its remedy.
18.sharh: The short word can name a person worn down by sickness or the lasting sickness itself. The second half turns from observing the sufferer to advising someone who can still seek treatment.

translation: When the noise of the times reaches you,
do not be slow to act.
19.sharh: Time makes a warning noise. The second noun gives the listener’s answer to that sound, speed in taking action.

translation: How often the dust is driven
toward more dust by the light-headed.
20.sharh: The short form can mean earth or dust swept along by the wind. Sending dust to join more of it is apt work for people whose defining quality is flightiness.

translation: Child of dust, the people around you
give you notice that they disown you.
21.sharh: The address claims earth as the listener’s nearest kin. Human beings deliver a very different message, the formal severing of a tie.

translation: I see blindness has come between
your eye and the clouds.
22.sharh: A cloud is large enough for anyone looking up to see. The loss of sight intervenes even between so conspicuous an object and the eye.

translation: Look for an eye salve for yourself
if you fear the day of banishment.
23.sharh: The short noun is a preparation used to clear the sight. The threatened departure in the rhyme turns looking ahead into a practical necessity.

translation: Eat the nightshade berries if you find
no lawful fare, for you are bound for extinction.
24.sharh: The berry of the nightshade is the speaker’s image of a last resource. Even the starkest effort to stay alive ends at the longer word, extinction.

translation: A mixed provision has often brought
those who packed it out onto open ground.
25.sharh: One old example of the short noun is dates mixed with raisins in a single container. A traveller can carry a long way the little mixture that equips him for the open country.

translation: May you be guided. Flee the blaze
if you have the wit to do so.
26.sharh: The blessing interrupts an urgent command. A person's intelligence is measured by the use made of it in getting clear of the flame.

translation: A man is very like an ass’s foal
if he gives no thought to obliteration.
27.sharh: An unthinking foal supplies the likeness. What a person can foresee, unlike the animal in the comparison, is even the disappearance of the traces a life leaves behind.

translation: Even the open plain will grow cramped
with people driven out of their prosperity.
28.sharh: Prosperity has a population that can lose its footing all at once. The poet imagines its former possessors so numerous that they might overfill an open plain.

translation: Ask your Lord for the gift
without which you cannot do.
29.sharh: The second half contains a negative. The reason for asking is that the listener has no independence from the very gift being sought.

translation: You leave instructions with your mind away in Bada.
No wonder your judgement keeps changing.
30.sharh: Bada gives the wandering mind a place to go. Its longer partner names a fresh view that displaces an earlier decision, making the instructions unreliable.

translation: It is as if the east wind
blew for those who chase youthful pleasures.
31.sharh: The wind has a compass point. The people have a taste for amusement. Their names sound close enough for him to imagine the wind itself in their service.

translation: They sold alertness for sleep.
Their wits are on the heights of Kara.
32.sharh: The bargain leaves the sleepers parted from their own judgment. A real place gives that absent judgment a faraway address.

translation: They are like goats with the head sickness,
or the brittle wreckage of reeds.
33.sharh: The commentary records a traditional name for a disorder of goats. Their loss of direction and the broken reeds' loss of strength furnish successive comparisons.

translation: How many bones in the curving sands
have parted from a fluttering standard.
34.sharh: The movement is all in the banner that once flew over them. Only their bones occupy the still ground at the bend of the sand.

translation: I see wealth calling the rich
to amusements and song.
35.sharh: Wealth does the inviting, the wealthy person is its guest, and song is the entertainment. Three linked sounds have three different parts in the scene.

translation: One hour of the night follows another,
while all he longs for is the water in his bowl.
36.sharh: Hours keep their own course while desire stays fixed on one small vessel. The short word names a unit of passing time, the long one something the hand could hold.

translation: How often men have been exposed,
beards and all, when the bark was stripped away.
37.sharh: Beards confer the appearance of dignity. On the studio’s reading, stripping the bark shows what lies beneath that appearance. A second gloss makes the men’s abusive quarrelling the thing exposed.

translation: How often enemies have caught
the hunter famed for taking game one animal after another.
38.sharh: The specialist term describes taking one animal hard upon another. The hunter with that enviable record has himself become the quarry of his enemies.

translation: How many structures stand deserted
after such refinement in their building.
39.sharh: One word names the finished structures, the other the costly care of making them. Desertion undoes the builder’s purpose without undoing the work.

translation: The people among the sweepings will be equal
to those who perfume themselves with incense.
40.sharh: The contrast can almost be smelled. People who lived among refuse and people who burned perfume converge at the same end.

translation: Many a well has water in abundance,
yet there is still need for a rope.
41.sharh: There is water enough, yet a rope is still needed to draw or carry it. Another commentary takes the second word as deliberation, something even a person with ample means may need.

translation: I see wear consume what is new,
and everything is destined to wear away.
42.sharh: Decay acts upon something still called new. Here the longer form can name that same wearing away, carrying the claim from one object to everything.

translation: How many an hour wears away the nights,
until, hour by hour, the nights themselves are gone.
43.sharh: The verse gives both jobs to an hour. It measures a small portion of a night, and by accumulating it measures the loss of every night. The printed commentary also understands the end as the moment when a thing has run its course.

translation: Even hospitality, I find, will not last
for ever with the giver of a guest’s meal.
44.sharh: The two vowel patterns name the same act of entertaining a guest. Even a lifelong host cannot keep his table set indefinitely.

translation: Someone other than the young man will inherit from him.
He will be taken from among those others.
45.sharh: The same idea of “other people” does two kinds of work. One of them receives the inheritance, and they are the company from which the dead man is taken. The rhyme can also mean their midst.

translation: Love of corruption ends in loathing.
I see nothing to hate in what is right.
46.sharh: The first attraction has an expiry date, the disgust that follows it. In the recited wording the second negative frees right conduct from that recoil. This is the first of three lines the reciter marks as doubtful in attribution.

translation: The water of life quenches thirst.
How can one driven from the trough ever drink his fill?
47.sharh: The word for someone driven from water belongs to the vocabulary of the watering place. A full supply is no comfort to someone denied access to it.

translation: How often have you seen the sunlight,
yet you shall not see the like of that radiance.
48.sharh: Both nouns are names for sunlight. The change is in the observer’s prospects, from many past sightings to uncertainty about seeing its like again.

translation: You long for an encounter that is forbidden,
though the day of meeting lies beyond it.
49.sharh: Both words mean meeting. One is an encounter the listener would choose, the other the appointed meeting before God.

translation: You have lived in a house with a roof.
You will certainly go out from under that covering.
50.sharh: The near-identical words both denote a covering overhead. The roof can remain in place even when death puts an end to the occupant’s tenure.

translation: Find glue for your arrow.
Shafts will not come right without glue.
51.sharh: An arrow maker needs adhesive to fix its feathers or fittings. A small piece of workshop knowledge makes memorable two forms for the same substance.

translation: Beware the heat of the fire of Hell.
It is the worst heat to be exposed to.
52.sharh: The ordinary vocabulary of standing close to a fire is pressed into the warning about Hell. The second form repeats the heat and intensifies its degree.

translation: The bloom of youth will leave you.
How little that youthful freshness ever availed.
53.sharh: The commentary glosses both nouns as the pleasures of youth. Once their passing is admitted, the question becomes how much lasting benefit they brought.

translation: I see that a ransom is beyond your power.
Who, then, will pay to redeem you?
54.sharh: In the recited pair a life is treated as though it could be bought back. The question exposes the absence of anyone able to pay the price.

translation: How often have you come to the pools,
then turned away from those same pools.
55.sharh: The traveller’s two actions are coming to water and departing from it. Two plural names for the pools let the same landscape serve at both ends of the journey.

translation: I see you gazing at a bat.
There is no good in watching a bat.
56.sharh: The eye stays on the same bat through the change of vowel and ending. Ibn Sida records both names for the animal. The printed commentary also gives a writing sheet for the first word and bark for the second.

translation: The morning sun has risen upon you.
You may never see the sun high later in the day.
57.sharh: The interval has shrunk to part of one morning. Surviving the early sun gives no assurance of living to see it approach noon.

translation: How often dreams come to nothing
for someone so fine to look at.
58.sharh: The two words turn sight in different directions. A handsome person may be pleasant for others to see and still find that his own dreams amount to nothing.

1.1.4.meaning: The pull of one's own desires.

1.2.3.head: الهَواء
1.2.3.meaning: The air around a living person, left behind at burial.

2.1.4.head: الثَّرى
2.1.4.meaning: Moist soil, here the earth of the grave.

3.1.5.meaning: The side or rim of a well.

3.2.3.head: الرَّجاء
3.2.3.meaning: Hope that a desired thing may come about.

4.1.3.head: الصَّفا
4.1.3.meaning: Broad, smooth stones. The singular is safah.

4.2.3.head: الصَّفاء
4.2.3.meaning: Purity of affection, friendship untroubled by ill will.

5.1.2.meaning: A young man, often with an implication of spirited generosity.

5.2.4.head: الفَتاء
5.2.4.meaning: The prime or vigour of youth, also its open-handed nobility.

6.1.2.head: السَّنا
6.1.2.meaning: Brightness, especially a flash or gleam of light.

7.1.4.meaning: Fresh grass, especially grass cut for fodder.

7.2.4.head: الخَلاء
7.2.4.meaning: An empty place or the solitude it affords.

8.1.2.head: النَّسا
8.1.2.meaning: The great vessel or sinew running down the leg, associated with sciatica.

8.2.4.head: النَّساء
8.2.4.meaning: Deferment or a reprieve. The first vowel is a.

9.1.2.meaning: Dimness of sight, especially in low light.

9.2.5.head: العَشاء
9.2.5.meaning: The evening meal, with initial a.

10.2.5.head: الخَواء
10.2.5.meaning: Vacancy, here a place empty of people.

11.1.3.meaning: The grounds immediately surrounding a dwelling or camp.

12.1.5.meaning: Soreness or tenderness of the foot from walking.

13.1.4.head: النَّقا
13.1.4.meaning: A mound or dune of sand.

14.1.2.meaning: A wild ass’s foal, or in another gloss a wild cow’s calf.

15.2.4.head: الحَياء
15.2.4.meaning: Modesty or a sense of shame.

16.2.4.head: الوَراء
16.2.4.meaning: Grandchildren or later descendants, those who come after a person. The same word also means “behind”.

17.1.4.head: النَّجا
17.1.4.meaning: The hide stripped from a sheep, or the act of flaying.

17.2.4.head: النَّجاء
17.2.4.meaning: Swift escape, the act of making off fast.

18.1.2.head: الدَّوى
18.1.2.meaning: Someone chronically sick, also the lingering illness itself.

18.2.5.head: الدَّواء
18.2.5.meaning: Medicine, the substance used for treatment.

19.1.3.meaning: A sound or din that reaches the listener.

20.1.3.head: السَّفا
20.1.3.meaning: Earth or windblown dust. The verse repeats this noun.

21.1.3.meaning: Dust. “Child of dust” relates the listener to earth.

21.2.3.head: البَراء
21.2.3.meaning: Disavowal or a declaration of being quit of someone.

23.1.4.meaning: A collyrium or eye preparation used to clear the sight.

23.2.5.head: الجَلاء
23.2.5.meaning: Departure from one's homeland, especially banishment.

24.1.2.meaning: The berries of the plant called fox-grape, a nightshade.

25.1.3.meaning: Mixed provisions, such as dates and raisins in one container.

25.2.3.head: الفَضاء
25.2.3.meaning: A wide expanse of open ground.

26.1.4.head: الذَّكا
26.1.4.meaning: The blaze or burning of a fire.

27.2.4.head: العَفاء
27.2.4.meaning: Effacement or obliteration, also the dust that covers a trace.

28.1.3.meaning: An open plain or broad stretch of desert.

28.2.3.head: المَلاء
28.2.3.meaning: Affluence or means. Another commentary reads a company of people.

29.1.4.meaning: A gift or favour one hopes to receive.

29.2.5.head: الجَداء
29.2.5.meaning: The ability to do without something.

30.1.4.meaning: Bada, a place-name. The early commentary locates it near Taif. The studio identifies a present-day Bada near al-Wajh.

30.2.4.head: البَداء
30.2.4.meaning: A change of mind when a new view presents itself.

31.2.3.head: الصَّباء
31.2.3.meaning: Youthful diversion or the pursuit of pleasure.

32.2.3.head: كَراء
32.2.3.meaning: Kara, a place in the Taif region. The verse refers to its heights.

33.1.3.meaning: An old name for a disorder affecting goats’ heads.

33.2.4.head: الأَباء
33.2.4.meaning: Reeds or reed canes, here their burnt or broken tips.

34.1.4.head: اللِّوى
34.1.4.meaning: A bend or tapering end in a stretch of sand.

36.1.2.meaning: An hour or watch of the night.

36.2.4.head: الإِناء
36.2.4.meaning: A vessel for food or drink.

37.2.5.head: اللِّحاء
37.2.5.meaning: Bark or an outer covering. An early gloss also gives abusive wrangling, another way the bearded men could be exposed.

38.2.5.head: العِداء
38.2.5.meaning: Taking one animal immediately after another in a single run.

39.1.3.meaning: Built structures, the plural of binya.

39.2.4.head: البِناء
39.2.4.meaning: Building or construction as an activity.

40.2.3.head: الكِباء
40.2.3.meaning: Incense, especially fragrant wood burned as perfume.

41.1.4.head: رِوى
41.1.4.meaning: An ample supply, enough water to quench thirst.

41.2.4.head: الرِّواء
41.2.4.meaning: A rope for securing a load or drawing water.

42.2.4.head: البَلاء
42.2.4.meaning: An alternate form for decay here. Elsewhere it can mean trial.

43.1.3.meaning: An hour of the night. The printed commentary also gives the time a thing reaches its limit.

43.2.4.head: الأَناء
43.2.4.meaning: An hour, likewise, with initial a and final hamza. It can also mean the reaching of a term.

44.1.2.meaning: The food set before a guest, hence hospitality.

44.2.5.head: القَراء
44.2.5.meaning: An alternative noun for entertaining or feeding a guest.

45.1.1.head: سِوى
45.1.1.meaning: Other than or someone else. The word can also mean the middle.

45.2.3.head: السَّواء
45.2.3.meaning: Others, the people from whom he is taken. The rhyme can also mean the midst or centre.

46.2.4.head: القَلاء
46.2.4.meaning: Loathing, the same sense in the longer form.

47.1.3.head: رِوى
47.1.3.meaning: A plentiful drink that quenches thirst.

47.2.3.head: الرَّواء
47.2.3.meaning: Sweet, thirst-quenching water, or drinking one's fill. Initial a.

48.2.5.head: الأَياء
48.2.5.meaning: Another form for the radiance of the sun.

49.1.2.meaning: An encounter or meeting, with initial u.

49.2.4.head: اللِّقاء
49.2.4.meaning: Meeting. The day of meeting is the day of reckoning.

50.1.4.meaning: A roof covering, traditionally of reeds and earth.

51.1.4.head: غَرا
51.1.4.meaning: An adhesive used, among other things, in making arrows.

52.1.2.meaning: The heat of a fire as it reaches the body.

53.1.1.head: جَرى
53.1.1.meaning: The freshness or enjoyment of youth.

53.2.5.head: الجِراء
53.2.5.meaning: Youthful vigour and enjoyment in the commentary’s gloss.

54.1.2.meaning: What is given to redeem a life or free a captive. The printed editions read a word for nourishment here.

54.2.4.head: الفِداء
54.2.4.meaning: Redemption by payment, or the ransom itself. The printed editions read a word for nourishment here.

55.2.4.head: الإِضاء
55.2.4.meaning: Another plural for a natural pool.

56.1.4.head: السَّحى
56.1.4.meaning: A bat, in the form with initial a and final long vowel. Another old sense is a sheet of writing material.

56.2.5.head: السِّحاء
56.2.5.meaning: A bat, also called by this form with initial i and final hamza. Another sense is bark or peel. The printed editions have “no harm” where al-Saeed says “no good”.

57.1.2.head: الضُّحى
57.1.2.meaning: Morning, once the sun has risen clear of the horizon.

57.2.5.head: الضَّحاء
57.2.5.meaning: Later morning as the day draws toward noon.

58.1.3.meaning: Visions or dreams, the plural of ru'ya.

58.2.4.head: الرُّواء
58.2.4.meaning: A goodly appearance or handsome bearing, with initial u.

20.2.2.head: السَّفا
20.2.2.meaning: The second use of dust, set against the abstract noun for folly.

36.1.4.meaning: Another span of time following the one before it.

47.2.2.head: المُحَلَّأ
47.2.2.meaning: Someone driven back from the watering place.
